{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=functional+self-awareness+architectures+epistemic+self-correction+assumptions&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.1093/9780197851708.003.0007\", \"title\": [\"Self-Aware Believing and Epistemic Akrasia\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>\\n                  <jats:p>This chapter argues that self-awareness will sometimes lead to cases of what is often thought of as rational epistemic akrasia. These are cases where subjects are rational to have a belief, while simultaneously rationally believing that they are not rational to have that belief. It concentrates on a certain kind of akrasia that can be induced by taking higher-order evidence seriously: examples where akratic subjects are rational to expect accuracy and rationality to diverge in their own cases. Using these cases, the chapter rejects arguments for the impossibility of rational akrasia. It also rejects some formal principles that would allow some degree of akrasia, but would place general limits on it. And it rejects the suggestion that akratic beliefs manifest some defect in the subject who has them.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1093/9780197851708.003.0007\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 9, 11]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1093/9780197851708.003.0006\", \"title\": [\"Self-Aware Believing and Epistemic Dilemmas\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>\\n                  <jats:p>This chapter argues that taking rational account of self-awareness results in “epistemic dilemmas.” These are cases in which rational requirements conflict with one another. The chapter discusses two kinds of strategies for avoiding dilemmas in our theory of rationality. The first avoids dilemmas by separating normative notions. The second avoids dilemmas by postulating indeterminacy about rationality. The chapter rejects both sorts of moves, in part by arguing that neither strategy avoids what might seem most troubling about dilemmas. It then argues that admitting dilemmas should not be seen as a problem. Instead, epistemic dilemmas should be seen as a natural and expectable consequence of rational self-awareness, and of taking HOE seriously.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1093/9780197851…

{"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=functional+self-awareness+architectures+meta-cognitive+evaluation+epistemic+error+correction&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"Predictive metacognition: a neuro-computational framework for self-monitoring in large language models.\", \"abstract\": \"Large Language Models demonstrate remarkable capabilities but suffer from critical metacognitive deficits, manifesting as overconfidence and hallucination, which severely limit their deployment in high-stakes applications. We introduce Predictive Metacognition, a neurobiologically-inspired framework that integrates principles of predictive processing and anterior cingulate cortex monitoring into transformer architectures. Our approach implements Error-Driven Learning and Dual-Process Monitoring through specialised fine-tuning that trains models to simultaneously generate responses and assess their own performance reliability. We fine-tuned Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Phi-3-Mini-4k-Instruct using LoRA (rank=8, [Formula: see text]) on 4,000 strategically constructed examples spanning varying confidence levels. Comprehensive evaluation against state-of-the-art baselines, including GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet, revealed statistically significant improvements in confidence calibration. Our metacognitive models achieved substantial reductions in Brier Score (11.6% and 17.2% respectively) and Expected Calibration Error ([Formula: see text], Cohen's [Formula: see text]). Critically, these improvements generalised robustly to out-of-domain tasks while maintaining competitive task accuracy. This work establishes a computationally tractable implementation of biologically-inspired metacognitive architecture for large language models, offering a principled pathway towards AI systems capable of reliable intrinsic self-monitoring that can more accurately assess their own knowledge boundaries and express appropriate uncertainty.\", \"doi\": \"10.1038/s41598-026-54840-2\", \"pmid\": \"42191827\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13434765\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-0…
